source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: A two-stage prompt (first devise a plan, then carry it out) is a machine version of the understand-plan-execute stages. Error analysis of zero-shot CoT found three failure types.
numbers: Zero-shot-CoT (GPT-3) error analysis: 46 failing GSM8K items in Fig 1. Table 6 (100 failing GSM8K items): Zero-shot-CoT calculation 7%, missing-step 12%, semantic 27%; Zero-shot-PS calculation 7%, missing-step 10%, semantic 26%.
quote: Let's first understand the problem and devise a plan to solve the problem.
limits: text-davinci-003, an old model. Semantic misunderstanding barely moves (27% to 26%), so planning does not fix misreading.
agent_relevance: Supports S1/S2 before S3: a plan step cuts missing steps but barely helps misunderstanding, so S1 needs its own check (restate, then verify the restatement).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Adding stage detail to the plan prompt (extract variables, compute intermediate results, mind calculation: PS+) gives larger gains than the plain plan prompt.
numbers: Zero-shot, text-davinci-003, six math sets, average accuracy: CoT 70.4, PS 73.5, PS+ 76.7. GSM8K: CoT 56.4, PS 57.0, PS+ 59.3. MultiArith: CoT 83.8, PS 92.2, PS+ 91.8. SVAMP: 69.9, 70.8, 75.7. AQuA 38.9, 43.9, 46.0.
limits: Gains are 3 to 6 points on average; GSM8K gain is only +2.9 for PS+. One 2022 model.
agent_relevance: A staged prompt costs few tokens and gives a few points; consistent with G11 and G7 (compare at equal tokens).

source: Kramer and Baumann (2024) Unlocking Structured Thinking in Language Models with Cognitive Prompting
finding: Prompting through human-like cognitive operations (goal clarification, decomposition, pattern recognition, generalization, integration) improves GSM8K. Variants: deterministic (D-CP), self-adaptive (SA-CP, model picks the sequence), hybrid with few-shot CoT (H-CP).
numbers: GSM8K test, LLaMA 3.1 8B/70B, Gemma 2 9B/27B, Qwen 2.5 7B/32B, 3 repetitions. H-CP reaches about 95% solve rate on LLaMA 70B. Most frequent self-chosen sequence on 70B: goal clarification, decomposition, pattern recognition (GC-DC-PR); shorter sequences dominate.
limits: Only GSM8K; baseline numbers are in plots, not text. Gain larger for mid-size models; Qwen 32B is already near ceiling zero-shot.
agent_relevance: When free to choose, the model picked short stage sequences. Fits a code-controlled graph where S1 to S3 is often enough; gain shrinks as the base model gets stronger (G12).

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: The revise stage (our S5) fails when the model itself must decide whether to revise. Earlier gains came from oracle labels that told the model when it was wrong.
numbers: With oracle label (GPT-3.5): GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 82.0, HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0. Without oracle, GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9, 75.1 (round 1), 74.7 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 75.8, 38.1, 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0, 25.0, 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; HotpotQA 49.0, 49.0, 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo with the 'report any serious problems' prompt: GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 and 90.0; CommonSenseQA 84.0 to 81.5 and 83.0.
quote: improvements vanish when oracle labels are not available
limits: Models up to GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2; 2023 era. RL-trained reasoning models may differ. Several feedback prompts were tried; none helped.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1 and G2: revise only on a code-detected failure. S4 TEST must come from code, not model self-judgement.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Why self-revision hurts: the model flips right answers to wrong more often than wrong to right. Multi-agent debate is also compared with plain self-consistency.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time; among changes, correct-to-incorrect exceeds incorrect-to-correct. On CommonSenseQA the model changes often because distractor options look relevant. Self-consistency GSM8K: 1 response 76.7, 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2.
limits: The debate rows of the table were garbled in text extraction; only self-consistency numbers are quoted here.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 (no debate) and G4. Cheap parallel samples plus a code vote beat critique loops.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: A generate, feedback, refine loop (a machine evaluate-and-revise stage) helps on taste-judged tasks but not on math.
numbers: Paper reports 20% absolute average gain over one-step generation. Dialogue response (GPT-3.5) 36.4 to 63.6; code readability 37.4 to 51.3; math reasoning 64.1 to 64.1 (no change). ChatGPT feedback was 'everything looks good' for 94% of math instances. With an external signal that the answer is wrong, math gains exceed 5 points (Appendix H.1).
limits: Many tasks are scored by GPT-4 preference, which favours longer revised text (verbosity bias, G5). Math gain is zero without an external error signal.
agent_relevance: Refinement helps where quality is fuzzy; for checkable tasks use code checks (G2, G3, G5).

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Self-feedback gains split by task type: large for preference-scored tasks, small or zero for single-answer tasks.
numbers: Dialogue +27.2 (GPT-3.5, 36.4 to 63.6); code readability +13.9 (37.4 to 51.3); code optimisation +8.2 in one model and +0.2 in another; math 0.
limits: Preference scores come from GPT-4 judging, same-family bias.
agent_relevance: Use stage loops for open-ended output only with a code or external judge; for exact tasks prefer sample-and-vote.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: An agent loop: act, get an external feedback signal, write a verbal reflection, store it in memory, retry. A look-back stage built into an agent, with an outside check.
numbers: ALFWorld +22 points absolute in 12 iterative steps; HotPotQA +20 points; HumanEval +11 points, pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%.
quote: reinforce language agents not by updating weights, but instead through linguistic feedback
limits: Gains rely on external feedback (unit tests, environment reward). Huang et al. show oracle-labelled loops overstate self-correction. HumanEval relies on model-written tests.
agent_relevance: Matches S4 (external test) to S5 to S9 (store a lesson). Keep the external-signal requirement (G2).

source: Gou et al. (2024, ICLR) CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Verify then correct using outside tools (search, code interpreter, toxicity API). The model's own critique alone adds almost nothing; tool output carries the gain.
numbers: ChatGPT: +7.7 F1 across three QA tasks, +7.0% absolute on three math program tasks, 79.2% lower toxicity probability. Ablation: self-critique alone gave -0.03 and +2.33 F1 (two LLMs). Gain over ReAct: +5.1 and +8.2 average F1.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Needs tool access. Tested on text-davinci-003, ChatGPT, LLaMA-2 only. The paper itself calls all tested LLMs unreliable verifiers.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2 and G3: do S8 VERIFY through a tool, not a model opinion.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
finding: Four stages: draft, plan verification questions, answer them independently (not seeing the draft), write the final answer. Independence of the verify step is the key design choice.
numbers: Wikidata list questions, Llama 65B few-shot: precision 0.17 to 0.36. Hallucinated answers per question 2.95 to 0.68; correct answers 0.59 to 0.38 (some true answers lost).
limits: Facts and lists, not reasoning chains. Reduces true answers too.
agent_relevance: Verification answered without the draft in view fits G5 (judge sees no proposed answer). Use for S8 on factual claims.

source: Weng et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification
finding: Backward verification: mask a condition in the problem, plug in the candidate answer, ask the model to recover the condition, rank candidates by match. A check by construction.
numbers: Average gain on Instruct-GPT 2.33%. Arithmetic tasks average gain 1.67% and 2.84% (two settings); other reasoning tasks 0.62% and 0.78%. K=5 candidates, P=10 verification samples each.
limits: Small gains, mostly arithmetic; costs 5x10 verification calls.
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-ranked form of S8, but small effect per token (G7).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024, TACL) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Survey of self-correction papers. Many positive results used oracle information or unfair baselines. Self-correction works with reliable external feedback or after fine-tuning for it.
numbers: Frames: realistic vs unrealistic and fair vs unfair frameworks. Cites negative results for intrinsic self-correction in arithmetic, closed-book QA and code generation.
quote: recent studies report negative results indicating that LLMs cannot self-correct
limits: A survey; claims come from the cited papers, no new runs.
agent_relevance: A checklist to judge any 'reflect and revise' stage we add; supports G2.

source: Lin et al. (2024) CriticBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Critique-Correct Reasoning
finding: 15 datasets in 5 domains, 17 LLMs tested on generation, critique and correction (GQC). Critique ability tracks generation ability.
numbers: Four findings: (1) linear relation among generation, critique and correction, and critique-focused training helps; (2) logic-oriented tasks are more amenable to correction; (3) knowledge inconsistency between generation and critique shrinks as models grow; (4) stronger models critique weaker ones better.
limits: Per-model scores are in figures and were not extracted; findings are qualitative here.
agent_relevance: A model's critique is only as good as its generation, so one model is a weak sole critic (G4, G8).

source: Jeong et al. (2026) Beneath the Surface of Chains-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Reasoning Operations in LLMs
finding: Reasoning text is split into operations grouped by Polya stage (understanding, planning, execution, look back). Operations are separable in hidden states, peaking in middle layers, in Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B and Gemma4-31B, not explained by wording or position.
numbers: Spans labelled by GPT-5; 84 spans checked by 7 humans: majority agreement on 81 of 84 (96.4%, Fleiss kappa 0.666); GPT-5 matched the human majority on 64 (76.2%, Cohen kappa 0.715). Data: DAPO-Math-17K plus a theorem set; 500 to 700 correct traces per model. Peak-layer one-vs-rest AUROC 'consistently high' (values in figure).
limits: Math only; LLM-labelled spans; separable representation does not prove the model follows a stage. Three open models.
agent_relevance: Evidence that stage labels are real structure in model states, not only prompt words. A probe could later detect which stage a trace is in.

source: Lee et al. (2026) Llama-Polya: Instruction Tuning for Large Language Model based on Polya's Problem-solving
finding: Fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B on dialogues that follow Polya's four stages changes how the model moves through stages. Generic models skip stages and give the answer at once.
numbers: Variants: instruct, metamath, polya-v2, metamath+polya-v2, on GSM8K-derived tutoring dialogues. Stage-protocol error rate: polya-v2 0.0%, metamath 0.4%; base and instruct higher, mostly bypassing stages and answering in one turn. Sequential metamath+polya-v2 also high (interference).
limits: Tutoring dialogue, not solving accuracy; 'error' is stage-protocol violation judged by annotators; small expert evaluation; fine-tuned, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Plain models jump past S1 and S2 to the answer. A code-enforced S1-to-S2 order fixes this without training; training variants can interfere.

source: Friedman et al. (2026) Not Too Short, Not Too Long: How LLM Response Length Shapes People's Critical Thinking in Error Detection
finding: Humans judging LLM reasoning on 15 modified Watson-Glaser items: accuracy depends strongly on whether the LLM explanation was correct; medium length helps most when it is wrong.
numbers: Within-subjects, N=24, 15 items, LLM output 42 to 150 words (mean 82.2). LLM wrong: participants correct 54% (medium), 25% (short), 31% (long). LLM right: highest accuracy 81% at medium length; predicted accuracy about 71% to 81% across lengths.
limits: Small N, length not manipulated apart from content, no no-LLM control, workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Humans over-trust fluent text, so any human review step should see short claim-level items.

source: Peczuh et al. (2025) Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills
finding: LLMs scoring critical thinking subskills in student argumentative essays against human coders. A fine-tuned small model beat prompted GPT-5. Subskills needing subtle distinctions scored worst.
numbers: Essay split, 5 seeds: Llama 8B fine-tune accuracy .604, RMSE .933, macro F1 .489, Krippendorff alpha .606; ModernBERT fine-tune .563; GPT-5 zero-shot .543, few-shot .532. Information Analysis subskills about .78 accuracy (skewed labels); Using Logical Fallacies accuracy .50 vs .61 for another subskill.
limits: Student essays, not model reasoning; low absolute accuracy; label skew inflates some scores.
agent_relevance: LLMs spot fallacies poorly (.50), so an LLM critic in S4 on arguments needs code or tool backing (G5).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: Large Language Models Self-Compose Reasoning Structures
finding: The model selects from atomic reasoning modules (including 'critical thinking' and 'break down into sub tasks'), adapts them, and writes an explicit structure that it then follows. A per-task choice of process stages.
numbers: Accuracy BBH: PaLM 2-L 56%, +CoT 60%, +Plan-and-Solve 61%, +Self-Discover 67%; GPT-4 58, 75, 73, 81. T4D: PaLM 2-L 30, 40, 42, 69; GPT-4 51, 52, 53, 85. MATH: PaLM 2-L 45, 42, 49, 50.5; GPT-4 70.5, 71, 70, 73. Claims 10 to 40x fewer inference calls than self-consistency-style methods.
limits: Structure chosen by the model with no check. MATH gain small (73 vs 71). 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Per-task stage choice helps most on algorithmic tasks (T4D +33 over CoT for GPT-4). Suggests S0 GATE should choose the stage subset by problem class.

source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought: Steering LLM reasoning with Argumentative Querying
finding: A pipeline from argumentation theory: plan with premises and conclusions, check eight critical questions from Toulmin's data, warrant and backing, accept only if 7 of 8 pass, retry, then answer by the plan. A machine critical-thinking check stage.
numbers: MT-Bench reasoning and math, LLM judge 1 to 10. Average gain +4.61% reasoning, +5.4% math. Llama 3.1 70B reasoning 8.05 baseline to 8.4 CQoT; math 8.95 to 9.55. Nemotron-51b reasoning 6.75 to 7.3; math 8.75 to 9.15. Plan-only ablation (steps 1 and 4): Llama 70B reasoning 8.3, math 9.25; Nemotron 6.85 and 9.0. Best in 18 of 20 comparisons plus one tie. Claude Sonnet 3.5 CoT equals CQoT on math; Nemotron CQoT worse than CoT on reasoning.
quote: Does the reasoning process avoid fallacies or logical errors?
limits: LLM judge (G5 bias); the check is a model self-check, which Huang et al. warn about; up to 10 loops raises cost; about half the gain comes from the plan-only steps.
agent_relevance: Best-measured critical-thinking stage pipeline for LLMs. Test with a code check instead of a self-check.

source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought: Steering LLM reasoning with Argumentative Querying
finding: Loop rule: need 7 of 8 yes for the first five loops, then 5 of 8, then proceed anyway after ten loops. A bounded stop that never abstains.
numbers: Limits 5 and 10 loops; thresholds 7/8 then 5/8. With CQoT the small Nemotron-51b scored above the Gemini 1.5 pro baseline on one task.
limits: Thresholds chosen by the authors, no ablation; the judge is the same model family.
agent_relevance: Matches G6 (never abstain) and a bounded loop; thresholds are [D] choices, to be tested.

source: Cross-paper synthesis of Plan-and-Solve, Cognitive Prompting and Self-Discover (all opened)
finding: In these stage-prompt papers the stage sequence is fixed or model-chosen. None enforces transitions with code or tests whether a stage output was good before moving on.
numbers: Plan-and-Solve +3.1 average points over CoT; Cognitive Prompting about 95% on LLaMA 70B (hybrid); Self-Discover +7 (PaLM 2-L) and +23 (GPT-4) BBH points over direct. All compare with zero-shot or CoT, not equal-token best-of-N.
limits: Reader synthesis, not a new measurement.
agent_relevance: Our G7 test is stricter than this literature: compare stage scaffolds to best-of-N at equal tokens.

source: Cross-paper synthesis of Huang 2024, Gou 2024 and Madaan 2023 (all opened)
finding: Three independent studies agree: the same model as its own judge gives near-zero or negative gain; outside signals give the gain.
numbers: CRITIC self-critique alone -0.03 and +2.33 F1; Huang intrinsic GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.9 to 74.7, GPT-4 95.5 to 89.0; Self-Refine math 64.1 to 64.1.
limits: Different tasks and models; numbers only roughly comparable.
agent_relevance: Three-source basis to mark G2 as established for the S4/S5 pair.

source: Synthesis of PS (2023) and Huang (2024): stages before the answer vs after
finding: Stages placed before the answer (plan, restate) show small gains; stages placed after the answer (self-review) do not, unless an outside signal exists.
numbers: Plan-and-Solve +3.1 average points before solving (70.4 to 73.5); Huang GSM8K GPT-3.5 75.9 to 74.7 after two review rounds.
limits: Different models and years; indirect comparison.
agent_relevance: Put effort in S1/S2 and external S4 checks; keep S5 conditional on a found failure.

source: Source lineage check across the opened LLM papers
finding: Of the stage-based LLM papers opened, only Self-Discover cites Polya in its text (as motivation for decomposition) and two 2026 papers build directly on Polya's four stages. None tests Dewey's phases or Hitchcock's list as a whole.
numbers: Opened: 16 papers. Polya central in 2 (Llama-Polya, mechanistic paper); Toulmin central in 1 (Critical-Questions-of-Thought); Dewey and Hitchcock in 0. Plan-and-Solve and Cognitive Prompting do not name Polya in the extracted text.
limits: Absence finding from papers opened here, not a literature-wide count.
agent_relevance: No LLM study tests a full Dewey/Hitchcock-style staged graph; each stage is tested piecewise. Our S1 to S9 graph would be a new test.

source: Search note: models on standard critical thinking tests (Watson-Glaser, Halpern, Cornell)
finding: One web search for GPT-class models taking the Watson-Glaser, Halpern or Cornell tests found no paper reporting model scores. It found only humans judging LLM text on Watson-Glaser items and LLM scoring of essays.
numbers: Related papers opened: Friedman 2026 (N=24, humans) and Peczuh 2025 (GPT-5 zero-shot essay scoring accuracy .543). Searches used: 2 of 6.
limits: One search only; absence is not proof. arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate limited (HTTP 429) so no second pass.
agent_relevance: Open gap: we could measure our agent on Watson-Glaser-style items ourselves as a baseline.

source: Synthesis: Self-Refine, Reflexion and CRITIC on the 'look back' stage S9
finding: Look-back loops that store a lesson (Reflexion) gain 11 to 22 points when the signal is external (tests, environment reward); loops that rely on the model's own judgement gain 0.
numbers: Reflexion +22 ALFWorld, +20 HotPotQA, +11 HumanEval; Self-Refine math 0; CRITIC self-critique +2.33 F1 at best.
limits: Reflexion's baselines and tasks differ from Huang's; tasks are checkable by tests.
agent_relevance: S9 lessons should be written only from code-found facts and stored for reuse in later attempts.
